value.text: The sound of bagpipes and taps filled the air Saturday as the Indian River County Sheriff’s Office unveiled a new memorial honoring two deputies killed in the line of duty.The memorial, located outside the sheriff’s office’s new administration building, honors Sgt. Terri Sweeting-Mashkow and Cpl. Their deaths happened 40 years apart. Now, their names have a permanent place together.WATCH: New memorial honors two Indian River County deputies killed in line of dutyThe unveiling came exactly one year after Sweeting-Mashkow was killed while serving an eviction notice at a home in the Bermuda Club community.47-year-old Sweeting-Mashkow was one of three deputies serving the eviction notice on Nov. 21, 2025, when authorities said 37-year-old Michael Halberstam retrieved a weapon and opened fire. Sweeting-Mashkow was killed, and Deputy Florentino Arizpe was shot in the shoulder.A locksmith who was there for the eviction, David Long, was also critically wounded and later died from his injuries.Sweeting-Mashkow had served with the Indian River County Sheriff’s Office for more than 25 years. Her death marked the second line-of-duty death in the 100-year history of the Indian River County Sheriff's Office.For those who gathered Saturday, the passage of a year has not made that loss feel distant.“It’s an honor to be out here but also very sad,” community member Joanne Knott said. “To think that it happened a year ago is strange because it feels like it was yesterday.”The memorial also reaches back four decades, honoring Cpl. Richard Raczkoski, who was killed in the line of duty 40 years ago.“The two heroes that are on this memorial are two people that our community will remember forever,” Indian River County Sheriff Eric Flowers said.Hundreds of family members, friends, law enforcement officers and community members gathered for Saturday’s unveiling, paying their respects.“I am so glad that they did this for Terri and Raczkoski,” one community member said.For those at the ceremony, the memorial is also a reminder of the risks law enforcement officers face each time they go to work.“All of these officers that step out into the community, they never know what their day is going to bring,” says Knott.Flowers hopes the two names on the memorial will be the only ones it ever bears: “I hope we never have to add names to this memorial again."

As if record rainfall wasn’t enough, severe storms Saturday night raced through our area from Palm Beach County through the Treasure Coast.A number of viewers reached out to us from the Bridges community in Delray Beach located off Lyons Road south of Atlantic Avenue.Christopher Daum told us he was prepping dinner when he heard the tornado warning alert on his phone.“All of a sudden it got super windy, super loud. My wife asked me to turn the water off, what was that noise. We looked in the back and saw trees blowing everywhere,” said Daum.There have been no reports of any major injuries as of 9 p.m. Saturday.Viewers sent us video of sheriff’s deputies blocking roads where trees had fallen in the Huntington Lakes community.You can send us your photos to newstips@wptv.com

Vice President JD Vance and Michigan Sen.-elect Abdul El-Sayed are preparing to meet, the incoming Democratic lawmaker and the White House said, after a bitter campaign season that featured sharp and at-times personal attacks between the two men.The circumstances of the would-be meeting were not immediately clear, nor was it certain on whose initiative it was being set. And Vance will ultimately preside over El-Sayed’s swearing-in Jan. El-Sayed said in a Tuesday interview on MSNOW that his team was contacted by Vance's office for a meeting. Vance’s office said Wednesday that it had contacted El-Sayed’s staff after being told the Democrat sought time with the vice president.RELATED STORY | Democrat Abdul El-Sayed projected to win Michigan Senate raceThe talk of a meeting comes as Vance nears a decision on whether to seek the Republican nomination for the White House in 2028, which has been complicated by voters' bruising rejection of President Donald Trump in this month's midterm elections, and as El-Sayed prepares to take office as the nation’s first Muslim senator.Both men have in recent days expressed willingness to attempt to find common ground after their heated criticism — albeit on their own terms. Vance described El-Sayed as “very, very evil" while campaigning for Michigan Republican Senate nominee Mike Rogers outside Detroit in August and appeared to question the Democrat's patriotism.Vance, however, sounded a much more charitable tone about the incoming Michigan senator during a Fox News Channel interview Monday.“If Abdul El-Sayed wants to work with me and the president to make people’s lives better, he’s going to find us very much a willing partner,” Vance said during the Fox segment.It was far from clear how and on what issues the two might cooperate, especially in light of El-Sayed's chief policy objective, a Medicare for All healthcare system the Trump administration, including Vance individually, has dismissed.RELATED STORY | Blue Jays distance team from Santander posts after El-Sayed’s Senate victoryBut it appeared at least to represent a rare bipartisan olive branch for President Donald Trump's attack dog in the wake of midterm elections, when Republicans were routed nationally while losing majorities in both houses of Congress, and as Vance looks ahead to his own future.“If he wants to work with us to get money out of politics, put money in pockets and pass Medicare for All, which is what I ran on, I'm a willing partner,” El-Sayed said on MS NOW.

Lucie family says it has spent nearly four years trying to get a swale liner installed to keep stagnant water from lingering in its yard, a problem the family says leaves water sitting for days and turns the property into what they jokingly call a "mosquito hotel."Oprah Fasulo and her mother, Divika Todd, brought the problem to WPTV's Michael Hoffman after meeting him at WPTV's Let's Hear It community meetup in Jensen Beach.Their frustration centers on a yearslong wait and changing rules over who is responsible for installing the swale liner. Now, the city says the family is not alone and that it recently received approval to add a contractor to help speed up installations.Fasulo and Todd told Hoffman their problem dates back to when their Port St. Lucie home was built.At the time, the city was changing its rules surrounding responsibility for installing swale liners, which are designed to help keep water moving rather than allowing it to remain on properties.According to the family, installation had been the city's responsibility before shifting to builders. It has since shifted back to the city.Their house, they said, was built between those changes and never received one.The family eventually contacted Port St. Lucie."They said that they have to install it. The homeowners are not allowed to install it," Fasulo said.Fasulo said she understood that requirement. What frustrated her was how long her family was told it would take."I understand that totally, but they told us that it was three years; it would be done," she said.Now, Fasulo said the family has been told it could take another two years.That's when they turned to WPTV."We've seen you guys get results," Fasulo told Hoffman.The family provided WPTV with pictures showing water collecting around the property even after lighter rainfall.They also walked Hoffman around their property to show him the problem firsthand.The standing water wasn't the only issue they encountered. Mosquitoes quickly made their presence known.Fasulo has a name for it."Mosquito hotel," she said.For the family, however, the nickname highlights a problem they've been trying to resolve for years: Water takes days to clear from their property, and they say they cannot install the needed liner themselves.Hoffman brought the family's concerns to the city and sat down with Scott Samples to ask why the process has taken so long and what is being done about it.Samples said the family is not the only one waiting."We were recently approved to add a contractor to help us to expedite getting some of these put in," Samples said.The city is also evaluating how to use its available resources to address the outstanding installations more quickly, Samples told WPTV."We're looking at, again, how can we maximize the resources that we have available to help the residents as quickly as we can, knowing that we're limited," Samples said. "You know, so we try to put this, there's plans, and then you have to adjust those plans as you go as well. So we're sort of in that process right now."For Fasulo and Todd, that still does not provide a date for when their swale liner will finally be installed.But after nearly four years of waiting, they now have WPTV asking those questions alongside them."You guys have helped in the past with this issue," Fasulo said. "So we decided to ask you guys to help us and whoever else is in need and not getting answers from the city."WPTV will continue following the family's case and pressing Port St. Lucie for updates on when the work will be completed.This story was reported on-air by a journalist and has been converted to this platform with the assistance of AI. Our editorial team verifies all reporting on all platforms for fairness and accuracy.

Nearly three weeks after historic flooding forced families from their homes and caused millions of dollars in damage across Martin County, residents are still waiting for a federal disaster declaration that could unlock critical financial assistance.Now, after a WPTV report on the delays and growing frustration among flood victims, Florida's top emergency management official is responding to questions about the state's recovery efforts—and what help families can expect if FEMA funding never arrives.Watch more from Kate Hussey:In an exclusive interview with WPTV investigative reporter Kate Hussey, Jared Perdue, director of the Florida Division of Emergency Management, confirmed the state submitted an expedited federal disaster declaration request Nov. 9, one week after the initial flooding.But nearly two weeks after that request, a decision remains pending."We've been very engaged with FEMA, and we did actually submit an expedited disaster declaration request to FEMA on November the ninth," Perdue said. "FEMA has been very closely coordinating with us in reviewing that, and I'm sure they're going to make quick work of it."The uncertainty comes as Martin County estimates approximately $18 million in residential and public infrastructure damage, with families still struggling to afford repairs and another round of historic rainfall complicating recovery efforts.Along Hyline Drive in Jensen Beach, the devastation is still visible.Dumpsters line driveways, waterlogged belongings have been discarded and homes have been stripped down to their frames.For Linda Weisbecker, whose home was among those severely damaged, the destruction has been overwhelming."It's like an apocalypse here," Weisbecker told WPTV in an earlier interview.For nine days, Weisbecker and her neighbors navigated waist-deep floodwaters before they could begin salvaging what remained of their homes."Once we got through that and the water came out, we just all started pitching in, going in to see what we can salvage from each home," she said.But much of what Weisbecker lost cannot be replaced."We are fully gutted. Our house is empty," she said. "We lost everything, from pictures of our children and their lives, our friends, our grandkids, now we have great-grandkids. Everything [my husband] had since he was 13 on is gone."Weisbecker has been approved for a $25,000 grant through Florida's State Housing Initiatives Partnership, or SHIP, program. But for families facing tens of thousands of dollars in repairs, that assistance may cover only a fraction of the cost.And not everyone will qualify."You do think about that process and you sit there and you say to yourself, how am I gonna do this?" Weisbecker said.That question is at the center of WPTV's ongoing investigation.Martin County estimates the flooding caused:$14 million in beach damage.Nearly $1 million in damaged roads requiring repaving.$3 million in residential losses.Additional expenses associated with county staff overtime and emergency response.A federal major disaster declaration could make certain public infrastructure repairs eligible for FEMA reimbursement and potentially open the door to individual assistance for qualifying residents.But approval is not guaranteed.When WPTV initially contacted FEMA, the agency confirmed it had received the disaster declaration request and that it remained under review. FEMA referred additional questions about the response and recovery timeline to the Florida Division of Emergency Management.Hussey subsequently pressed Perdue on what would happen if the federal government denied the request."If FEMA ultimately denies federal assistance, does Florida have a Plan B, or are these families simply on their own?" Hussey asked.Perdue did not identify a specific alternative state funding program, instead emphasizing Florida's experience responding to natural disasters and its ongoing coordination with federal and local officials."This is something that we're very used to doing. I mean, in Florida, we deal with natural disasters all the time," Perdue said. "We have a great relationship with FEMA, and usually those things go very well."He added that the state remains focused on immediate response efforts, including search and rescue operations and meeting residents' emergency needs.In the meantime, Martin County is working to distribute approximately $1 million in available SHIP funding to qualifying residents.Eligible homeowners may receive grants of up to $25,000, with additional assistance potentially available through loans of up to $75,000. However, those loans come with repayment requirements and liens.Income eligibility restrictions could also leave some families without assistance, even if they cannot afford to rebuild on their own."There's going to be a lot of heart-wrenching cases where somebody barely missed the limit," Commissioner Blake Capps said during a recent Martin County Commission meeting.Capps proposed establishing a separate county-funded emergency assistance program for residents who fall through the cracks.But when WPTV asked where that money would come from, Capps acknowledged a funding source had not yet been identified."Well, that would be ... we'd have to talk to staff," he said.County Human Services Director Michelle Miller previously told commissioners the state had promised additional disaster relief funding, although neither the amount nor the timeline had been confirmed."They haven't confirmed the amount yet but has assured us we will be getting some disaster relief funds," Miller told Hussey.Hussey raised those concerns directly with Perdue, asking whether the state had other programs available for families who earn too much to qualify for existing assistance but not enough to pay for repairs.Perdue pointed to the state's partnerships with nonprofit organizations and its deployment of emergency personnel to assist with cleanup."We've actually activated the National Guard, and are also partnering with nonprofits to do what they call the muck and gut of homes that have been flooded," Perdue said.That work includes removing damaged drywall and other waterlogged materials to help prevent mold growth."We're providing the assistance that we can and partnering with those nonprofit organizations as well," he said.However, Perdue did not identify a specific funding program to cover rebuilding costs for homeowners who do not qualify for existing assistance.The financial uncertainty extends beyond individual homeowners.Martin County faces approximately $15 million in combined beach and road damage, with additional emergency response expenses still being assessed.County spokesperson Martha Ann Kniess previously told WPTV that without federal reimbursement, Martin County could be left responsible for covering those costs, potentially forcing officials to redirect money from elsewhere in the budget or identify other funding sources.Hussey asked Perdue whether the state would help cover those expenses if FEMA denied federal assistance — or whether the financial burden could ultimately fall on local taxpayers.Perdue did not commit to providing state funding for those repairs."We are and have been doing damage assessments ever since we submitted the first disaster declaration request," he said."As those damage assessments come in, we'll continue to coordinate with FEMA and make sure all that information is submitted."The state's response follows an emotional Martin County Commission meeting Tuesday, where residents pleaded with elected officials to do more to secure recovery funding."Please. Fight for us!" one resident urged commissioners.Others questioned why families were being asked to wait even longer for answers."And the answer from this dais is wait 13 more days?!?" another resident asked.Commissioner Eileen Vargas said she had reached out to FEMA through personal contacts in an effort to expedite the process."I did, through contacts, reach out to FEMA to try and get this going," Vargas said.Vargas also told residents she expected a new FEMA director to take office Nov. 30 and hoped that development could help move the disaster declaration forward.But even if a declaration is approved, not all losses or recovery expenses would necessarily qualify for federal assistance.As Martin County continues to recover from the Nov. 2 flooding, Perdue said the state is also responding to another significant rainfall event affecting communities across Florida.According to Perdue, Gov. Ron DeSantis expanded the state's emergency executive order to include 21 counties.The state has mobilized resources from the National Guard, State Guard, Florida Highway Patrol and Florida Fish and Wildlife Conservation Commission, among other agencies."We're actively still responding to the previous flooding event on November 2, and now we're actively dealing with a current, another historic rain event that's brought record amount of flooding in many counties throughout the state," Perdue said.The overlapping disasters have added urgency to recovery efforts, particularly for residents whose homes remain exposed after being gutted.Perdue said state resources remain available for immediate needs, including food, water, shelter and emergency medical assistance."We're committed. We're fully mobilized," he said. We're going to be with you till the very end, and we're going to make sure we help everybody get back on their feet."Despite those assurances, several critical questions remain unresolved.FEMA has not announced a decision on Florida's expedited disaster declaration request. The state has not identified a specific alternative rebuilding assistance program for homeowners who do not qualify for existing aid, nor has it committed to covering Martin County's public infrastructure losses if federal funding is denied.For residents like Weisbecker, the uncertainty is more than a question of government funding.It's a question of whether they can afford to return to the homes they've spent years building their lives in."This is very urgent for people to get back into their daily lives," Weisbecker said. "This is total devastation.

Three years after the movie theater at CityPlace was demolished, the big screen is planned to make a comeback in downtown West Palm Beach.WATCH: Related Ross shares new details on CityPlace movie theaterDeveloper Related Ross is working to bring a new movie theater to downtown as part of its planned 515 Fern building, near the Brightline station. Current plans call for eight auditoriums and about 800 seats.For people who live in and frequent downtown West Palm Beach, the announcement answers something many say has been missing.Hannah Alexander lived downtown for two years before recently moving to Boynton Beach. She said going to the movies while living downtown often meant leaving the city.“We actually used to live right in downtown, and we'd have to travel all the way to Palm Beach Gardens to watch movies, and so I think it would be great,” Alexander said. “We're actually here just to hang out in this area because we really like it, so we’d definitely come.”Alexander said she used to go to the movies a couple of times a month, but the lack of a nearby theater has made that more difficult.“Honestly, recently I haven't gone to the movies because I don't want to have to drive to the movie theaters,” she said.Her boyfriend, Alec Estrill, agreed.“Yeah, the commute is kind of annoying, you know, especially when you're so close to downtown, you would like something more local to attend,” Estrill said.Even after moving to Boynton Beach, the couple said a movie theater could give them another reason to return downtown.“Of course, yes, definitely,” Alexander said. “I think it'd also be cool for the residents because when we lived here we did a lot of things just walking in the area and be able to commute by bike or walking. That would be great for the residents that are still here.”Jordan Rathlev, executive vice president of Related Ross, said those reactions mirror what the developer has been hearing over the past year.“It's amazing, the reception,” Rathlev said. “I think we anticipated they were going to embrace this. This is an exciting opportunity for us to bring a great entertainment complex back to the downtown.”Rathlev said the decision followed months of conversations with people living in West Palm Beach.“We've been meeting with a number of groups, including the Downtown Neighborhood Association and the West Palm Beach Resident Coalition, and they've all said, ‘We want a theater, we want more entertainment, we want more things that our residents, our neighbors can go to.’ And we said, ‘Yeah, we agree with you.’”Rathlev, who also lives in West Palm Beach, said the desire for more family-friendly entertainment downtown became personal.“I mean, frankly, I'm a resident. I've lived here for almost 10 years. I have a 9- and 7-year-old. They want to go to the movies,” Rathlev said. “So we said, look, where can we find opportunities for things that families can do? Not just businesses and people from out of town, but what can the local residents really enjoy? And theater continued to be one of those things that we heard continuously from people that they wanted back here.”That's one of the biggest remaining questions.Related Ross has not selected an operator for the theater, but Rathlev said conversations are underway.“We're talking to all the operators. They see a tremendous opportunity with everything that's happening in and around West Palm,” Rathlev said. “So we're excited that we'll be able to announce one of the great premier operators in the country wanting to plant their flag here in West Palm.”When asked whether a decision has been made, Rathlev responded, “No decision made yet.”But some potential moviegoers already have a wish list.Downtown resident Rob Coppinger said he would like to see something beyond a traditional movie theater.“A higher-end theater, like an iPic-type thing, where they're serving food, things like that, would be great,” Coppinger said.And when it comes to the screen?“I guess the bigger screens, the better, right?” he said.Caleb Suppner, who was visiting CityPlace with his daughter Mia, also said he would like to see a dine-in experience.“Yeah, I mean, she loves the dine-in kind of vibe ones, like the new ones, you know, where you can have lunch, dinner, even the adults can grab a drink,” Suppner said.Mia had an even more specific request.“I like the 3D ones when it feels like when the chairs are moving and it looks like when the stuff come out in real life,” she said.WPTV took that request directly to Rathlev, asking if a theater with a big screen and moving seats could happen.“We're definitely open to it. We'll look at all opportunities,” Rathlev said. “We want to make every resident feel like this is their theater and really embrace it, and we're looking forward to it.”Rathlev said the developer wants the new theater to take advantage of how much the movie-going experience has evolved.“The technology is evolving so much, whether it's the seats or the way you watch the screens, whether it's 3D, whether it's interactive,” he said. “We're looking at all options, and we think this is an opportunity to really take advantage of the emerging technologies in the theater business.”Moviegoers will still have to wait.The 515 Fern building had previously been approved, but Related Ross is now going back through the approval process to incorporate the movie theater into the project.“We just started the reapproval process of the building,” Rathlev said. “It was approved two years ago, but we're now integrating this theater concept into it. We hope to have the approvals by the end of next year to be open in 2030.”For Rathlev, there's already one thing he's looking forward to most if those plans become reality.“Take my kids to the movies,” he said.This story was reported on-air by a journalist and has been converted to this platform with the assistance of AI. Our editorial team verifies all reporting on all platforms for fairness and accuracy.

A controversial proposal to build a more than 1.6 million-square-foot data center just half a mile from an elementary school is drawing growing opposition in Martin County, where residents are raising concerns about everything from environmental impacts to whether they'll have a say in the project's approval.WATCH: 'We need answers': Martin Co. officials address outrage over proposed data centerOn Friday morning, a small but vocal group of residents gathered outside the Martin County Administrative Center, demanding answers about the massive development proposed for a parcel of land off Kanner Highway, west of Interstate 95.They had planned to attend a meeting with the county's Growth Management Department. But less than 17 hours before it was scheduled to begin, the county canceled it, citing overwhelming public interest.Residents showed up anyway."We need answers, and we need them quick," said Chris McIntyre, whose son graduated from nearby Crystal Lake Elementary School. "This story cannot die, or else this is the death of Crystal Lake School."McIntyre, who goes by Coach Mack, became emotional discussing what the proposed development could mean for the school and surrounding neighborhoods."Now that's the death of an A-rated elementary school that I love," he said, his voice breaking.He's far from alone.Residents have raised concerns about potential noise pollution, water consumption, increased electricity demand, higher utility bills, wildlife displacement, declining property values and possible health impacts on children attending Crystal Lake Elementary.Michael Panella, another resident opposing the project, became emotional while explaining why the fight is so personal."It's life. These little ones are innocent," Panella said, referring also to students of Crystal Lake. Dan Wilson, president of the Locks Landing homeowners association, represents a community less than two miles from the proposed site.“They’re probably dropping now because, oh, the data center going there. We don’t want to move there,” Wilson said of property values."We have residences right here, tons of residents. We're all going to have to deal with this."Residents acknowledge they don't yet know for sure what the long-term consequences of the project might be. They don't know whether electricity bills will increase, how much noise the facility could generate or what wildlife habitat might be lost.But they do know that once something of this magnitude is built, there's no easy way to undo it.The controversy intensified Thursday evening when Martin County announced the cancellation of an informal Growth Management meeting scheduled for 9:30 a.m. 19, the Martin County Board of County Commissioners posted the following message online:For residents who had planned to attend, the cancellation only added to their frustration."The thing that frustrates me the most about this is the fact that they were willing to do this meeting in private," said resident Alisha Gibbs.Gibbs described herself as "disgusted" and "absolutely appalled" by the situation.But Martin County Deputy Growth Management Director Pete Walden told WPTV Investigative Reporter Kate Hussey that the meeting was never intended to be a formal public hearing or a decision-making session.Instead, Walden said, it was an informal meeting requested by members of the public who wanted to ask county staff questions about the development — something his department routinely accommodates for other projects.He said information about the meeting circulated online, creating the impression that county officials were privately considering a decision on the data center.When interest grew beyond what the county could accommodate, officials decided to cancel."We could not accommodate that. We didn't have any rooms or anything available for that size," Walden explained. "So we had to cancel, and we'll do some workshops in the future. I believe the applicant is also going to reach out for some public presentations on the subject." When asked why residents weren't being given more opportunities to weigh in, Walden maintained the county has been transparent."We are transparent through the process, and everything can be made available to anyone that is interested," he said.Walden said additional public meetings and workshops will be scheduled to allow residents to ask questions and learn more about the project.But the canceled meeting is only one of several controversies surrounding the development.Another major point of contention is the timing of the developer's application.On Oct. 27, Martin County commissioners approved a one-year moratorium on data centers, temporarily restricting new applications while the county reviews its development regulations.But records show the application for this project was submitted the day before the moratorium was proposed on October 13. That timing means the project is not subject to the temporary restriction, according to county officials.Walden acknowledged the timing but said the county cannot control when developers submit applications."They obviously saw like everybody else that a moratorium was coming, and they got their application in ahead of time," Walden said. "We don't direct applicants ... and we certainly can't pick and choose when these things happen."WPTV reached out to the project applicant and the law firm representing it, requesting comment on the timing of the application and residents' environmental, energy and health concerns.Neither responded by publication time.Perhaps the most significant concern for opponents is whether residents will have any formal say in the project's approval.Under a county ordinance adopted in 2010, during the Great Recession, Martin County established an administrative approval process for certain targeted industries to encourage economic development.Data centers fall within the county's targeted industry classifications. According to Walden, the proposed development is also covered by an existing planned unit development, or PUD, agreement that allows qualifying targeted industries on platted industrial lots to receive administrative approval.That means the project could potentially move forward without a public hearing or recorded vote by county commissioners.For residents demanding a voice in the decision, that distinction is critical.Hussey asked Walden whether there was anything the county could do to give residents more of a say in whether the development is approved."With the moratorium, we'll be looking at our code to make revisions so everything is appropriately reviewed as it comes in," Walden said."To give the public more of a say in future projects?" Hussey asked. "Correct," Walden responded. Residents are also demanding answers about how a development of this size could affect surrounding neighborhoods, wildlife and students at Crystal Lake Elementary School.The proposal initially called for just under 1 million square feet of development. An updated application brings the total to approximately 1.6 million square feet, including an existing warehouse.Among the concerns raised by residents are the potential effects of noise from cooling equipment, increased water and electricity consumption, wildlife habitat loss and possible impacts on nearby property values.Those concerns remain questions, not established consequences of the proposed development.Walden said the county will review the project's potential impacts before making any approval decision.He also emphasized that despite speculation circulating in the community, the data center has not been approved."There is a misconception that this project was already approved — that's very far from the truth," Walden said."This is our first data center to be reviewed. We're going to take our time ... and make sure everything is properly vetted."The county says a staff report examining the project is expected to be released in December.Following that report, officials plan to schedule a public forum, likely including a presentation from the applicant, where residents can ask questions and learn more about the development.No date for that meeting has been announced.For opponents, the controversy goes beyond whether a data center belongs on acres of industrial land.It's about who gets to decide what their community becomes — and whether the people who will live with the consequences have a meaningful opportunity to influence that decision.The residents who gathered outside the county building Friday made clear that canceling a meeting would not end their opposition."If they want to actually please the public, they would deny this proposal," Gibbs said.

A couple of large department stores are now topping the list of the best places to shop for Black Friday deals, according to WalletHub.JCPenney and Macy's ranked No. 2 on the list, with deep discounts.And the Black Friday deals have started early, with some retailers offering discounts before Halloween.The top 10 stores and their average discounts from the WalletHub study for 2026:JCPenney: 74.33%Macy's: 56.50%Target: 38.47%Kohl's: 37.47%Best Buy: 30.88%Walmart: 30.57%BJ's: 30.51%Home Depot: 30.33%Amazon: 28.25%Newegg: 23.15%“Does not surprise me at all. Their sales have been fantastic this week,” said shopper Sarah Hanson in Wellington.“It's become Black November, essentially,” said Chip Lupo of WalletHub.Saving at least 30% is generally viewed as a good barometer of finding a Black Friday deal.However, Lupo says it may be worth waiting to shop for some gifts.“Things like electronics, laptops, phones, you could probably even get a better deal the closer you get to the end of the year, particularly if the manufacturer's got a new line of products coming in January,” he said.

Just as Gardino Nursery was beginning to recover from weeks of flooding, another round of rain has left the Loxahatchee Groves business underwater again.WPTV reporter Christy Waite has been following the flooding's impact on the nursery, touring the property several times and seeing the changing conditions firsthand.Watch report from Christy Waite:When Waite first visited Gardino Nursery a few weeks ago, floodwater covered much of the property. Water reached up to her shins in some areas, and fish could even be seen swimming through the floodwater.On Wednesday, Waite returned and found a much different scene. The standing water had largely receded, though thick mud still covered parts of the nursery. Owner Sid Gardino said at the time that conditions were finally improving. But the relief didn't last.After more rain fell, Gardino Nursery flooded again. Waite returned to the property and found plants submerged and standing water once again covering areas that had only recently begun drying out."This is the worst that I have seen on this property," Gardino said.Sid Gardino, owner of Gardino, said it was especially frustrating to see the flooding return after conditions had finally started moving in the right direction."We dried out a little bit, it started looking good and then the rain comes again and floods the whole place again," he said.The flooding is only the latest weather challenge for Gardino Nursery, an appointment-only plant nursery specializing in Hoyas, orchids, rare and unusual tropicals, fragrant plants and pre-bonsai.A year of weather extremes, including freezes, drought and repeated flooding, has kept the nursery closed to visitors since October."This is the 5th time that this has happened," Gardino said.During Waite's previous visit, Gardino told WPTV that the prolonged closure had already cost the business several thousand dollars in revenue.Now, he's also dealing with damage to some of the plants and trees he has spent years growing."I'm frustrated because it never ends. I lost a few very important trees here, I lost them because the water saturated the roots," he added.The repeated flooding has left Gardino with few options other than waiting for conditions to improve."I have to be patient and get a few good days so things can dry out and we can go back to full-time work because right now it is impossible," Gardino said.

The National Weather Service canceled a Flood Watch for Indian River County Friday morning, but additional showers remain possible and flooding continues to affect roads across the county. See also: DeSantis expands Florida emergency order to 21 counties amid flooding The heaviest rainfall threat is farther north, according to an update from Indian River County Emergency Services. Officials are asking drivers to check road conditions before traveling, allow extra time for detours and never drive through flooded roads. Friday, flooding or roadway damage was affecting these locations: U.S. 1 near Barber Street: Partial blockage Old Dixie Highway SW: Flooding and partial blockages at several locations 82nd Avenue at the entrance to Heritage Plantation: Partial blockage Skyline Drive, from Periwinkle to Barber Street: Partial blockage 130th Street: Closed 79th Street west of 130th Avenue: Closed because of a roadway washout 13th Street SW east of 66th Avenue SW: Closed because of roadway damage Vero Lake Estates: 104th Avenue between 87th and 93rd streets, and 83rd Street between 91st and 93rd avenues, are closed The county said the list includes selected locations. Drivers can check the live road closure map for additional closures and updates. Officials said water needs time to recede and damaged roads must be assessed and repaired before they can safely reopen. Crews are working in affected areas, and drivers are asked to give them room and follow barricades. Palm Beach County Schools will be closed on Friday, Nov. 20 due to forecasted heavy rainfall and the risk of flooding, the district announced on Thursday. After-school activities will also be cancelled. Part of Glades Road in west Boca Raton flooded after storms moved through Wednesday night into Thursday morning. However, the notice came after some students had already arrived on campus. In a message to families, Principal Edmund Capitano apologized for the disruption and inconvenience, saying, "We want to make sure all students and staff are able to leave campus safely this morning before the flooding continues to worsen." By Thursday evening, Palm Beach County Schools announced all schools would close Friday as officials continue monitoring weather conditions. Lucie Public Schools is also playing it safe, extending its closure through Friday after calling off classes Wednesday. The district said the heaviest rain is forecast during Friday’s morning arrival period. With the ground already saturated, officials warned of possible roadway flooding and hazardous travel. The decision comes after the district faced criticism for keeping schools open following record rainfall that flooded neighborhoods two weeks ago. Images from that storm showed a student walking through floodwaters after getting off a school bus. "We could see up to eight inches of rain, and we'd have flooding, and it'd be difficult to transport our kids, especially back home safely," St. Lucie Public Schools Superintendent Dr. "We don't want to be back in that ballpark again." Aftercare, activities and athletic events are also canceled Friday. Lucie Public Schools said it will announce later Friday whether Saturday’s SAT will go ahead. Students are scheduled to return Monday, Nov. 30, after Thanksgiving break. Indian River County public schools will also be closed Friday. The district cited localized flooding, saturated ground and the chance of more heavy rain. It said road closures are increasing, particularly in Vero Lake Estates, and rising water is affecting its North County Transportation compound. Schools there are scheduled to reopen Nov. 30, after Thanksgiving break. An Indian River County School District spokesperson said administrators will determine in the coming days whether missed instructional time will need to be made up. Schools in Martin and Okeechobee counties are expected to remain open Friday, though both districts said they will continue monitoring conditions. The Martin County School Board voted this week to reinstate Matthew Theobald, a teacher at Spectrum Academy, after a judge ruled his social media posts about conservative activist Charlie Kirk’s death did not justify suspension or termination. Theobald was initially targeted by the Martin County School District for several online comments following Kirk’s murder in Utah in September 2025. The school board voted to suspend Theobald without pay and recommended his termination. Both parties agreed to an administrative hearing to address the matter. In June, the judge ruled that the school board failed to prove Theobald engaged in immorality or willful neglect of duty, which would have been grounds for dismissal. The judge also stated that Theobald’s Facebook comments did not disrupt his students, the learning environment, or reduce any teacher’s ability to teach. Stay up-to-date: The latest headlines and weather from WPBF 25 Martin County School District leadership responded to the ruling by saying it would review the judge’s recommendation. This week, the school board officially voted to adopt the judge’s recommendation, rescinding Theobald’s suspension and termination. He will also be awarded back pay and benefits through June 30. School board member Marsha Powers said she voted in favor of the decision but explained her reasoning. “I have serious concerns about the process that brought this matter before a judge who does not live or work in the community,” Powers said. Get the latest news updates with the WPBF 25 News app. Board member Tony Anderson responded to Powers’ comments, saying he understood her concerns but noted the board had already placed the issue in the judge’s hands. “It’s a decision we have to live with,” Anderson said. WPBF 25 reached out to Matthew Theobald for comment but has not yet received a response.

The Indian River County Sheriff’s Office is reporting more flooded roads in the Vero Lake Estates area as heavy rain moves through the county Thursday. The sheriff’s office urged drivers to stay off flooded roads, warning that water can be deeper than it appears and can stall vehicles. High-water vehicles are in the area, and anyone who becomes stranded should call 911. Ryan Lloyd, Indian River County’s emergency management chief, told CBS12 News the county has received about 5 to 7 inches of rain so far. He said the north end of the county, including Sebastian, Fellsmere and Vero Lake Estates, has gotten more than the rest. Another 3 to 5 inches is expected by midnight Friday, Lloyd said, and the area is still at risk for pockets of 10 to 12 inches or more falling in a short time. Lloyd said the county’s water management systems are full and the ground is essentially saturated, so new rain is running off onto roads. The county’s emergency operations center is at a Level 2 partial activation, and National Guard members are there with high-water vehicles. Lloyd said there had been no requests for high-water rescues as of Thursday afternoon. He urged residents to avoid nonessential travel, turn around at flooded roads and never drive around barricades. Please do not drive to neighborhoods that are flooded because that can actually push floodwaters into homes and create a bigger problem than what some of those residents may already be facing, Lloyd said. The weather prompted the School District of Indian River County to close all public schools and district offices Thursday. The district said saturated ground and expected rain could make travel unsafe for students and staff. Lloyd said schools will also be closed Friday. A Vero Beach football game scheduled for Friday night has been moved to Saturday at 7 p.m., he said. The advisory warned of minor flooding in low-lying and poorly drained areas. A flood watch remains in effect for Indian River County through Friday evening, with more showers and thunderstorms possible. Among the roads marked closed were 100th Court, 103rd Avenue, 104th Avenue, 83rd Street and 87th Street. The map also showed a long-term closure on 13th Street Southwest, scheduled to remain in place until Jan. Lane-closure listings included 101st Avenue, West 98th Avenue and two locations near Barber Street and U.S. The county also warned that heavy rain and gusty winds could disrupt trash collection. Residents whose streets are flooded were asked not to put carts in the water; the landfill and customer convenience centers could close early if conditions become unsafe. The City of Fellsmere also urged drivers to use extreme caution, identifying two potential trouble spots: New York Avenue near Hickory Street and North Broadway. The city said those roads could close if rain continues. City Hall remains open and operating normally. Lloyd said there are no known water main breaks or significant power outages in the county. Even though the latest round of flooding is tapering off, the problems are only beginning for drivers whose cars were flooded. Rosalie Barrios is learning a costly lesson, the hard way.Barrios says she had no idea her car was about to be overtaken by water when she was driving home from her nursing job earlier this month. When she turned into her neighborhood, the water seemed manageable, until it wasn't."All of a sudden the car just sank, the water came in, and I was panicking," said Barrios.Within hours, her car conked out. The engine was waterlogged and ruined.Ron Katz, owner and mechanic of a MIDAS location in West Palm Beach, said nearly 10 gallons of water seeped into Barrios' engine. He flushed it out, but says the car was too far gone.Since the beginning of the month, Katz has serviced a handful of flooded cars. He's only been able to save one. He said the biggest mistake drivers make when they get caught in floodwaters is not letting it be and calling a tow truck."Human nature is, you're going to try and start your car, but the engine will hydrolock from the water being in the engine, and it'll just blow a hole through the engine," says Katz.Katz has taken to social media this month to warn readers not to try and start their vehicles if they find themselves trapped in high water.It's something Barrios wishes she'd known. She says her insurance company declared her car a total loss. Because she still owes on it, she's now underwater again."I invested a lot of money, and the car was running fine. I have nothing again," says Barrios.

A historic Vero Beach neighborhood is getting a new life through art, as sculptor Ross Power leads an effort to transform Edgewood into a vibrant community of artists, galleries, studios and public gathering spaces.Known as the "Father of the Vero Beach Art Village," Power is helping turn a once-overlooked neighborhood into a destination for creativity, where artists can live, work and share their talents.WATCH REPORT BELOW: The transformation is already underway, with murals, public art and community projects taking shape. And we have projects; there's a bunch of different projects we’ve been working on whether it’s for the city or for trying to save big blue, or our community garden, “ said Linwood Addison Fuller IV, an artist who moved to Edgewood for the focus on art. His wife is also an artist.“It’s so much better to be an artist in a community with other artists,” said sculptor Andrew Draminski. “I’m sitting here working and my neighbors are walking their dog down the alley and come on in and we have a cup of coffee or something like that.”The village's vision extends beyond traditional galleries. Organizers hope to create spaces for music, dance, poetry, photography, workshops and other community events.More galleries, studios and community spaces plannedAccording to the nonprofit Friends of the Vero Beach Art Village, the neighborhood's transformation is a grassroots effort involving artists, residents, businesses and volunteers.The organization highlights ongoing initiatives involving murals, public art, studios, galleries, streetscape improvements and community events.Power says additional galleries, studios, cafes and bed-and-breakfasts are also in the works.For him, the goal isn't simply to attract visitors. It's to create a community where artists can thrive together and residents can take pride in their neighborhood."If you want to eat great food, hear great music, see great things, meet great artists, this is the place," Power said.And beneath the sprawling branches of that century-old lychee tree, Power hopes the community he's helping cultivate will continue to grow.Where is the Vero Beach Art Village?The Vero Beach Art Village is located in the historic Edgewood neighborhood, just west of downtown Vero Beach.The neighborhood generally stretches between 14th and 20th avenues and 18th and 20th streets.The Friends of the Vero Beach Art Village nonprofit encourages residents and visitors to support the effort through volunteering, donations and participation in community art projects.Click here for more information about the village, its projects and opportunities to get involved.This story was reported on-air by a journalist and has been converted to this platform with the assistance of AI. A controversial proposal to build a more than 1.6 million-square-foot data center just half a mile from an elementary school is drawing growing opposition in Martin County, where residents are raising concerns about everything from environmental impacts to whether they'll have a say in the project's approval.WATCH: 'We need answers': Martin Co. officials address outrage over proposed data centerOn Friday morning, a small but vocal group of residents gathered outside the Martin County Administrative Center, demanding answers about the massive development proposed for a parcel of land off Kanner Highway, west of Interstate 95.They had planned to attend a meeting with the county's Growth Management Department. But less than 17 hours before it was scheduled to begin, the county canceled it, citing overwhelming public interest.Residents showed up anyway."We need answers, and we need them quick," said Chris McIntyre, whose son graduated from nearby Crystal Lake Elementary School. "This story cannot die, or else this is the death of Crystal Lake School."McIntyre, who goes by Coach Mack, became emotional discussing what the proposed development could mean for the school and surrounding neighborhoods."Now that's the death of an A-rated elementary school that I love," he said, his voice breaking.He's far from alone.Residents have raised concerns about potential noise pollution, water consumption, increased electricity demand, higher utility bills, wildlife displacement, declining property values and possible health impacts on children attending Crystal Lake Elementary.Michael Panella, another resident opposing the project, became emotional while explaining why the fight is so personal."It's life. These little ones are innocent," Panella said, referring also to students of Crystal Lake. Dan Wilson, president of the Locks Landing homeowners association, represents a community less than two miles from the proposed site.“They’re probably dropping now because, oh, the data center going there. We don’t want to move there,” Wilson said of property values."We have residences right here, tons of residents. We're all going to have to deal with this."Residents acknowledge they don't yet know for sure what the long-term consequences of the project might be. They don't know whether electricity bills will increase, how much noise the facility could generate or what wildlife habitat might be lost.But they do know that once something of this magnitude is built, there's no easy way to undo it.The controversy intensified Thursday evening when Martin County announced the cancellation of an informal Growth Management meeting scheduled for 9:30 a.m. 19, the Martin County Board of County Commissioners posted the following message online:For residents who had planned to attend, the cancellation only added to their frustration."The thing that frustrates me the most about this is the fact that they were willing to do this meeting in private," said resident Alisha Gibbs.Gibbs described herself as "disgusted" and "absolutely appalled" by the situation.But Martin County Deputy Growth Management Director Pete Walden told WPTV Investigative Reporter Kate Hussey that the meeting was never intended to be a formal public hearing or a decision-making session.Instead, Walden said, it was an informal meeting requested by members of the public who wanted to ask county staff questions about the development — something his department routinely accommodates for other projects.He said information about the meeting circulated online, creating the impression that county officials were privately considering a decision on the data center.When interest grew beyond what the county could accommodate, officials decided to cancel."We could not accommodate that. We didn't have any rooms or anything available for that size," Walden explained. "So we had to cancel, and we'll do some workshops in the future. I believe the applicant is also going to reach out for some public presentations on the subject." When asked why residents weren't being given more opportunities to weigh in, Walden maintained the county has been transparent."We are transparent through the process, and everything can be made available to anyone that is interested," he said.Walden said additional public meetings and workshops will be scheduled to allow residents to ask questions and learn more about the project.But the canceled meeting is only one of several controversies surrounding the development.Another major point of contention is the timing of the developer's application.On Oct. 27, Martin County commissioners approved a one-year moratorium on data centers, temporarily restricting new applications while the county reviews its development regulations.But records show the application for this project was submitted the day before the moratorium was proposed on October 13. That timing means the project is not subject to the temporary restriction, according to county officials.Walden acknowledged the timing but said the county cannot control when developers submit applications."They obviously saw like everybody else that a moratorium was coming, and they got their application in ahead of time," Walden said. "We don't direct applicants ... and we certainly can't pick and choose when these things happen."WPTV reached out to the project applicant and the law firm representing it, requesting comment on the timing of the application and residents' environmental, energy and health concerns.Neither responded by publication time.Perhaps the most significant concern for opponents is whether residents will have any formal say in the project's approval.Under a county ordinance adopted in 2010, during the Great Recession, Martin County established an administrative approval process for certain targeted industries to encourage economic development.Data centers fall within the county's targeted industry classifications. According to Walden, the proposed development is also covered by an existing planned unit development, or PUD, agreement that allows qualifying targeted industries on platted industrial lots to receive administrative approval.That means the project could potentially move forward without a public hearing or recorded vote by county commissioners.For residents demanding a voice in the decision, that distinction is critical.Hussey asked Walden whether there was anything the county could do to give residents more of a say in whether the development is approved."With the moratorium, we'll be looking at our code to make revisions so everything is appropriately reviewed as it comes in," Walden said."To give the public more of a say in future projects?" Hussey asked. "Correct," Walden responded. Residents are also demanding answers about how a development of this size could affect surrounding neighborhoods, wildlife and students at Crystal Lake Elementary School.The proposal initially called for just under 1 million square feet of development. An updated application brings the total to approximately 1.6 million square feet, including an existing warehouse.Among the concerns raised by residents are the potential effects of noise from cooling equipment, increased water and electricity consumption, wildlife habitat loss and possible impacts on nearby property values.Those concerns remain questions, not established consequences of the proposed development.Walden said the county will review the project's potential impacts before making any approval decision.He also emphasized that despite speculation circulating in the community, the data center has not been approved."There is a misconception that this project was already approved — that's very far from the truth," Walden said."This is our first data center to be reviewed. We're going to take our time ... and make sure everything is properly vetted."The county says a staff report examining the project is expected to be released in December.Following that report, officials plan to schedule a public forum, likely including a presentation from the applicant, where residents can ask questions and learn more about the development.No date for that meeting has been announced.For opponents, the controversy goes beyond whether a data center belongs on acres of industrial land.It's about who gets to decide what their community becomes — and whether the people who will live with the consequences have a meaningful opportunity to influence that decision.The residents who gathered outside the county building Friday made clear that canceling a meeting would not end their opposition."If they want to actually please the public, they would deny this proposal," Gibbs said.

A road and nearby property in Port St. Lucie have partially collapsed following historic flooding, leaving residents concerned about the growing damage and the safety of surrounding homes. “All this was flooded,” said Yoshi Duran, a neighbor who showed the damaged area near her home. From aerial views, the extent of the collapse is clear, with sections of the road and property having fallen into the hole. “It’s not anything to laugh about. It is a dangerous situation because they’re not knowing when it can cave in,” Duran said. The collapse occurred during the flooding, as water poured in and the land buckled until it finally gave way. Duran said the hole has been expanding daily since then. Because what’s going to happen, you know? What’s going to happen to the houses that are around this area?” Duran said. City officials are aware of the issue and are working to address it. “We want to repair these as quickly as we possibly can. Unfortunately, it takes some time,” said Scott Samples, public information officer for Port St. Samples explained the damage was caused by excess water both on the road and in a culvert below it. He said the city is currently determining the best way to fix the problem. “You want to make sure you’re doing it as well and as correctly as you possibly can. So that may require some studies to take place before you actually start the work,” Samples said. For Duran, that work can’t come soon enough. We understand everybody is short-staffed. But we need answers,” Duran said. City officials said there is no timeline for the repairs since they're still trying to figure out the best way to fix the problem. Just weeks after historic flooding destroyed homes and displaced families in Jensen Beach, Martin County residents are bracing for another round of heavy rain — with up to 12 inches forecast over the next three days.For families still struggling to recover, the threat of more flooding comes as county commissioners work to determine what caused the initial disaster and how to help those who lost nearly everything.On Tuesday, flood victims packed a Martin County Commission meeting, pleading for financial assistance and answers.WATCH REPORT BELOW: Along Cheri Drive in Jensen Beach, the signs of destruction remain. Dumpsters line driveways, damaged belongings sit outside and families are still trying to salvage what's left of their homes.Lisa French, her husband, Jeremy, and their two young sons are among those displaced after floodwaters rose as high as 3 feet inside some homes two weeks ago."It's like we're kind of stuck," French told WPTV investigative reporter Kate Hussey. French said her home had about 3 to 6 inches of flooding that sat inside for more than a week, causing mold to grow 3 to 4 feet up the walls. "So they, yeah, they tore the walls down in the house," said French. "They just chipped up the last bit of the tile, and it's empty." Now, with more rain approaching, French fears her family could face another disaster before recovering from the first."Of course, we're afraid because we all flooded in our houses," she said.New figures released by Martin County show at least 36 homes sustained damage, with an estimated $3 million in residential losses. Commissioners estimated another $14 million in damage to beaches, and at least $1 million in damage to roadways that now need repairs. For some residents, the destruction represents a lifetime of memories washed away."We've lost everything," one elderly Jensen Beach resident told commissioners. "We have 60 years of our life — kids, grandkids, everything. It's all gone."As residents demand answers about what went wrong, commissioners approved shifting $200,000 from the county's stormwater budget to investigate whether development and changes to local drainage systems contributed to the flooding.Commissioner Blake Capps called the investigation "a good starting point.""It may be that we need to augment the study beyond the $200,000 that we approve today," said Capps. Meanwhile, county crews are working around the clock to prepare for the next storm, lowering retention pond levels, deploying additional pumps and draining flooded properties."We have people 24 hours a day pumping that material down," Martin County Public Works Director Jim Gorton said.Commissioners also approved financial assistance for eligible flood victims through the state's State Housing Initiatives Partnership (SHIP) program.The assistance includes grants of up to $25,000 for income-eligible homeowners and loans of up to $75,000 secured by liens on their properties.But there's a catch: The grants are reimbursement-based, meaning homeowners must first pay for eligible repairs before receiving the money.For families who lost everything, that presents another obstacle."We don't have $25,000," French said. "A lot of people don't have $25,000, so it's great, and we're appreciative, but I mean, our house is empty, and $25,000 is not going to do much for us." The other problem: the county currently has just $1 million in SHIP funding available, and commissioners warned the money could run out quickly, even with additional state funding promised."They haven't given us the amount yet, but they have assured us that we will be getting some disaster relief funds," said Human Services Director Michelle Miller Strict income limits could also disqualify some flood victims who cannot afford to rebuild on their own. The income cap for a family of one is $86,040. The cap for a family of two is $98,400. For a family of four, it's $122,880. When reporter Kate Hussey asked Capps what would happen to those families, he acknowledged the county needs to explore other options."There are going to be a lot of heart-wrenching cases where someone barely missed the limit, and we're going to need to take a look at what we can do for those folks," Capps said.For residents like French, the need is immediate."We just need somebody to step up," she said. "We need funding." With another round of heavy rain approaching, Martin County is distributing sandbags at Halpatiokee Regional Park to help residents protect their properties, with a limit of 25 per person. The County's Emergency Operations Center is scheduled to be staffed beginning Tuesday at 2 p.m., and the county is coordinating with the National Weather Service and Florida Division of Emergency Management (FDEM).Fire Rescue is also standing by with multiple high-water rescue trucks.Commissioners also said a Federal Emergency Management Agency representative is expected to visit Nov. 30 to assess the damage — a potential step toward securing federal disaster assistance.But for families still displaced and facing the possibility of more flooding, the uncertainty remains.

Nearly three weeks after historic flooding forced families from their homes and caused millions of dollars in damage across Martin County, residents are still waiting for a federal disaster declaration that could unlock critical financial assistance. Now, after a WPTV report on the delays and growing frustration among flood victims, Florida's top emergency management official is responding to questions about the state's recovery efforts—and what help families can expect if FEMA funding never arrives. Watch more from Kate Hussey: In an exclusive interview with WPTV investigative reporter Kate Hussey, Jared Perdue, director of the Florida Division of Emergency Management, confirmed the state submitted an expedited federal disaster declaration request Nov. 9, one week after the initial flooding. But nearly two weeks after that request, a decision remains pending. "We've been very engaged with FEMA, and we did actually submit an expedited disaster declaration request to FEMA on November the ninth," Perdue said. "FEMA has been very closely coordinating with us in reviewing that, and I'm sure they're going to make quick work of it." The uncertainty comes as Martin County estimates approximately $18 million in residential and public infrastructure damage, with families still struggling to afford repairs and another round of historic rainfall complicating recovery efforts. Along Hyline Drive in Jensen Beach, the devastation is still visible. Dumpsters line driveways, waterlogged belongings have been discarded and homes have been stripped down to their frames. For Linda Weisbecker, whose home was among those severely damaged, the destruction has been overwhelming. "It's like an apocalypse here," Weisbecker told WPTV in an earlier interview. For nine days, Weisbecker and her neighbors navigated waist-deep floodwaters before they could begin salvaging what remained of their homes. "Once we got through that and the water came out, we just all started pitching in, going in to see what we can salvage from each home," she said. But much of what Weisbecker lost cannot be replaced. Our house is empty," she said. "We lost everything, from pictures of our children and their lives, our friends, our grandkids, now we have great-grandkids. Everything [my husband] had since he was 13 on is gone." Weisbecker has been approved for a $25,000 grant through Florida's State Housing Initiatives Partnership, or SHIP, program. But for families facing tens of thousands of dollars in repairs, that assistance may cover only a fraction of the cost. And not everyone will qualify. "You do think about that process and you sit there and you say to yourself, how am I gonna do this?" Weisbecker said. That question is at the center of WPTV's ongoing investigation. Martin County estimates the flooding caused: A federal major disaster declaration could make certain public infrastructure repairs eligible for FEMA reimbursement and potentially open the door to individual assistance for qualifying residents. But approval is not guaranteed. When WPTV initially contacted FEMA, the agency confirmed it had received the disaster declaration request and that it remained under review. FEMA referred additional questions about the response and recovery timeline to the Florida Division of Emergency Management. Hussey subsequently pressed Perdue on what would happen if the federal government denied the request. "If FEMA ultimately denies federal assistance, does Florida have a Plan B, or are these families simply on their own?" Hussey asked. Perdue did not identify a specific alternative state funding program, instead emphasizing Florida's experience responding to natural disasters and its ongoing coordination with federal and local officials. "This is something that we're very used to doing. I mean, in Florida, we deal with natural disasters all the time," Perdue said. "We have a great relationship with FEMA, and usually those things go very well." He added that the state remains focused on immediate response efforts, including search and rescue operations and meeting residents' emergency needs. In the meantime, Martin County is working to distribute approximately $1 million in available SHIP funding to qualifying residents. Eligible homeowners may receive grants of up to $25,000, with additional assistance potentially available through loans of up to $75,000. However, those loans come with repayment requirements and liens. Income eligibility restrictions could also leave some families without assistance, even if they cannot afford to rebuild on their own. "There's going to be a lot of heart-wrenching cases where somebody barely missed the limit," Commissioner Blake Capps said during a recent Martin County Commission meeting. Capps proposed establishing a separate county-funded emergency assistance program for residents who fall through the cracks. But when WPTV asked where that money would come from, Capps acknowledged a funding source had not yet been identified. we'd have to talk to staff," he said. County Human Services Director Michelle Miller previously told commissioners the state had promised additional disaster relief funding, although neither the amount nor the timeline had been confirmed. "They haven't confirmed the amount yet but has assured us we will be getting some disaster relief funds," Miller told Hussey. Hussey raised those concerns directly with Perdue, asking whether the state had other programs available for families who earn too much to qualify for existing assistance but not enough to pay for repairs. Perdue pointed to the state's partnerships with nonprofit organizations and its deployment of emergency personnel to assist with cleanup. "We've actually activated the National Guard, and are also partnering with nonprofits to do what they call the muck and gut of homes that have been flooded," Perdue said. That work includes removing damaged drywall and other waterlogged materials to help prevent mold growth. "We're providing the assistance that we can and partnering with those nonprofit organizations as well," he said. However, Perdue did not identify a specific funding program to cover rebuilding costs for homeowners who do not qualify for existing assistance. The financial uncertainty extends beyond individual homeowners. Martin County faces approximately $15 million in combined beach and road damage, with additional emergency response expenses still being assessed. County spokesperson Martha Ann Kniess previously told WPTV that without federal reimbursement, Martin County could be left responsible for covering those costs, potentially forcing officials to redirect money from elsewhere in the budget or identify other funding sources. Hussey asked Perdue whether the state would help cover those expenses if FEMA denied federal assistance — or whether the financial burden could ultimately fall on local taxpayers. Perdue did not commit to providing state funding for those repairs. "We are and have been doing damage assessments ever since we submitted the first disaster declaration request," he said. "As those damage assessments come in, we'll continue to coordinate with FEMA and make sure all that information is submitted." The state's response follows an emotional Martin County Commission meeting Tuesday, where residents pleaded with elected officials to do more to secure recovery funding. Fight for us!" one resident urged commissioners. Others questioned why families were being asked to wait even longer for answers. "And the answer from this dais is wait 13 more days?!?" another resident asked. Commissioner Eileen Vargas said she had reached out to FEMA through personal contacts in an effort to expedite the process. "I did, through contacts, reach out to FEMA to try and get this going," Vargas said. Vargas also told residents she expected a new FEMA director to take office Nov. 30 and hoped that development could help move the disaster declaration forward. But even if a declaration is approved, not all losses or recovery expenses would necessarily qualify for federal assistance. As Martin County continues to recover from the Nov. 2 flooding, Perdue said the state is also responding to another significant rainfall event affecting communities across Florida. Ron DeSantis expanded the state's emergency executive order to include 21 counties. The state has mobilized resources from the National Guard, State Guard, Florida Highway Patrol and Florida Fish and Wildlife Conservation Commission, among other agencies. "We're actively still responding to the previous flooding event on November 2, and now we're actively dealing with a current, another historic rain event that's brought record amount of flooding in many counties throughout the state," Perdue said. The overlapping disasters have added urgency to recovery efforts, particularly for residents whose homes remain exposed after being gutted. Perdue said state resources remain available for immediate needs, including food, water, shelter and emergency medical assistance. We're fully mobilized," he said. We're going to be with you till the very end, and we're going to make sure we help everybody get back on their feet." Despite those assurances, several critical questions remain unresolved. FEMA has not announced a decision on Florida's expedited disaster declaration request. The state has not identified a specific alternative rebuilding assistance program for homeowners who do not qualify for existing aid, nor has it committed to covering Martin County's public infrastructure losses if federal funding is denied. For residents like Weisbecker, the uncertainty is more than a question of government funding. It's a question of whether they can afford to return to the homes they've spent years building their lives in. "This is very urgent for people to get back into their daily lives," Weisbecker said. "This is total devastation.

Lucie family says it has spent nearly four years trying to get a swale liner installed to keep stagnant water from lingering in its yard, a problem the family says leaves water sitting for days and turns the property into what they jokingly call a "mosquito hotel." Oprah Fasulo and her mother, Divika Todd, brought the problem to WPTV's Michael Hoffman after meeting him at WPTV's Let's Hear It community meetup in Jensen Beach. Their frustration centers on a yearslong wait and changing rules over who is responsible for installing the swale liner. Now, the city says the family is not alone and that it recently received approval to add a contractor to help speed up installations. Fasulo and Todd told Hoffman their problem dates back to when their Port St. At the time, the city was changing its rules surrounding responsibility for installing swale liners, which are designed to help keep water moving rather than allowing it to remain on properties. According to the family, installation had been the city's responsibility before shifting to builders. It has since shifted back to the city. Their house, they said, was built between those changes and never received one. The family eventually contacted Port St. "They said that they have to install it. The homeowners are not allowed to install it," Fasulo said. Fasulo said she understood that requirement. What frustrated her was how long her family was told it would take. "I understand that totally, but they told us that it was three years; it would be done," she said. Now, Fasulo said the family has been told it could take another two years. That's when they turned to WPTV. "We've seen you guys get results," Fasulo told Hoffman. The family provided WPTV with pictures showing water collecting around the property even after lighter rainfall. They also walked Hoffman around their property to show him the problem firsthand. The standing water wasn't the only issue they encountered. Mosquitoes quickly made their presence known. "Mosquito hotel," she said. For the family, however, the nickname highlights a problem they've been trying to resolve for years: Water takes days to clear from their property, and they say they cannot install the needed liner themselves. Hoffman brought the family's concerns to the city and sat down with Scott Samples to ask why the process has taken so long and what is being done about it. Samples said the family is not the only one waiting. "We were recently approved to add a contractor to help us to expedite getting some of these put in," Samples said. The city is also evaluating how to use its available resources to address the outstanding installations more quickly, Samples told WPTV. "We're looking at, again, how can we maximize the resources that we have available to help the residents as quickly as we can, knowing that we're limited," Samples said. "You know, so we try to put this, there's plans, and then you have to adjust those plans as you go as well. So we're sort of in that process right now." For Fasulo and Todd, that still does not provide a date for when their swale liner will finally be installed. But after nearly four years of waiting, they now have WPTV asking those questions alongside them. "You guys have helped in the past with this issue," Fasulo said. "So we decided to ask you guys to help us and whoever else is in need and not getting answers from the city." WPTV will continue following the family's case and pressing Port St. Lucie for updates on when the work will be completed.
